title: The Incarnation and the Humiliation of the Word
english: than the angels, so that we in him might be enriched with what is beyond our own nature, by the good pleasure of God the Father. For he "raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ" (Ephesians 2:6). Since Christ, the Savior of us all, sits enthroned with the Father, the boast will run through the whole of human nature. Otherwise, how have we been made rich by his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9), if our condition was in no way raised to something better when the one who is above all creation became one of us? So he was made a little lower than the angels by becoming man, in order to honor the nature of man and to bring it back to what it was at the beginning, being crowned with glory and honor in it as well, though as God he is the Lord of glory. For just as Adam's transgression showed us to be utterly without honor, so we have been glorified through the obedience of Christ on our behalf, who laid down even his own life "so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living" (Romans 14:9).

How was he made lower than the angels, he who is worshiped by them? Was it not that he came down into the measures of humanity, took a body that by nature dies, and suffered in it willingly; and that he is crowned with the highest glories because of the suffering, as having abolished death through it and made corruption powerless, since he is incorruption and life? The angels' advantage is that they are outside the flesh and above dying, while the Son came to be in these things through his voluntary self-emptying. But the one made a little lower than the angels because of the measure of humanity, being in the supremacy of the Godhead, is worshiped by them, and he is seated on thrones around which they stand, glorifying him always and naming him Lord of the powers.

"So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone" (Hebrews 2:9). What "he tasted for everyone" means is clear, I think. For he gave his own body to death and, so to speak, tasted in the flesh what befell it; then he came back to life and at once trampled down the power of death. So the one said to have been made a little lower than the angels is the Word who is from God himself. He did not suffer the lessening in his own nature, for he is always himself and the same, unchangeable and unalterable; but he underwent this too for our sake, in a human way. For though he is God by nature, he put up with the measures of humanity for the sake of the economy. And this, in the mystery that concerns him, is what most deserves our wonder. So too the prophet Habakkuk said, "Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was amazed" (Habakkuk 3:2). For what took place is truly an amazement, beyond all wonder. Yet somehow certain people, not having understood the mystery concerning him rightly, talk emptily, and have even written, wanting to interpret what is in the eighth psalm:

"Let us consider, then, who is the man at whom he is astonished and marvels that the Only-begotten deigned to remember him and to visit him." Then to this he adds, and very plainly, that "What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" (Psalm 8:4) is not said of every man, but of the Son alone. They try to make their own words firm and to pass them off as truth by saying that the blessed Paul applied the words of the psalm to his person, because he says, "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). Then, dividing the natures, they say that the one born of the holy Virgin is wholly a man in his own right; it is at him, they say, that David marvels, that he was thought worthy of remembrance and of visitation, and was thought worthy also of what is beyond his own nature, as one who receives benefits from God the Word. But they have failed to see, it seems, that Christ Jesus is not thought of or spoken of by us as a man by himself, either in the common or in the individual sense, but rather as the Word from God made man. title: Divine Promise and Human Nature
english: may be seen to proceed in due order, come, before anything else let us take up the interpretation of the psalm we have mentioned. The inspired David knew as a prophet that, according to the unlying and divine promise, one would be born "of the fruit of his loins according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30); yet he was well aware that, being God by nature, he would let himself down into our condition in due time. So in the eighth psalm he converses with him and addresses his words to him as to man and at the same time God, recognizing as one God the one who is from both. That is why he says, "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty is lifted up above the heavens" (Psalm 8:1). For where at all, or among whom, was Christ not wondered at? Or how was his majesty, and the splendor of his glory, not lifted up even above the heavens, if indeed it is true that "at the name of Jesus Christ every knee bows, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:10-11)?

That the inspired singer says such things to the Word, who appeared in human form and was united to flesh, what follows would easily show. For he said, "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise" (Psalm 8:2). When he had raised Lazarus from the dead, he was wondered at by all, and "finding a young donkey, he sat on it" (John 12:14); and then the children took "the branches of the palm trees" (John 12:13) and honored him with the acclamations due to him, saying, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" (Matthew 21:9). When others rebuked them, Christ said, "Have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?" (Matthew 21:16). So, seeing the Son made man and all but riding on the colt, David was rightly astounded, as he pondered this: that one who is God by nature is seen to have let himself down to so great a lowliness. Then, seeing no other reason for the self-emptying than us alone, whom it was necessary to rescue from corruption and sin and to snatch from the tyrant's hands (I mean the devil's), the blessed David holds the mystery of the economy in the flesh worthy of all wonder. That is why he says, "Lord, what is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" (Psalm 8:4). For what is the nature of man compared with God? And why do I say this? What is the human race? And at what share would those on earth be reckoned, compared, I mean, with the ranks of the holy angels? But even if man is nothing at all, in nature and in number, the Creator did not overlook us. He remembered us too and thought us worthy of his visitation, as men who had perished; he who at the beginning, when he brought us into being, made us a little lower than the angels, but crowned us with honor and glory, set us over the works of his hands, and put all things in subjection under our feet (Psalm 8:5-6).

Such is the aim of the whole song. But the inspired Paul reasons very deeply, and with great skill he turns our sick condition around into newness through Christ. For what is in him is a new creation: the old things have passed away, and all things have become new (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Holy Spirit says this through one of the prophets too: "Take heart, Zion, let your hands not grow slack. The Lord your God is in you, mighty to save you, and he will renew you in his love" (Zephaniah 3:16-17). So Paul shows that we are stripped of the glory given us long ago; that is why he says, "But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him" (Hebrews 2:8). Since we have chosen to think rightly, we surely do not think that he says such things about one man. Rather, signifying man in general as in one person, he says that he has been robbed of his share in the renown given long ago. title: Incarnation
english: that man has fallen short of the glory through the transgression in Adam, so that he may also describe the way it is recovered; and he makes plain how poor the race was, so that he may show in turn the one through whom we have been made rich. For he adds at once, "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). For the Word from God, being God by nature, as we have said very often, let himself down into self-emptying and was counted among us as a man, a little lower than the angels, so that, having become obedient to the Father even to death (Philippians 2:8), he might crown the nature of man with glory and honor, being crowned as one of us, though he is the Lord of glory.

But if someone were to say that the man born of the holy Virgin was thought worthy of remembrance and visitation by God the Word, and was benefited and thought worthy of honor beyond his own nature, he will bring the glory of the mystery down, as it were, to the ground, and he will earn a great deal of ridicule. For tell me, where is Christ a mere man? When is he thought of apart from the Word united to him? He is Emmanuel from the womb, and this did not come about by stages. How then do they say that he was thought worthy of visitation and remembrance by God the Word? Then, by dividing and separating him entirely, they would also be caught setting him apart, showing us another Christ and Son, stripped of the Word united to him. For the one who thought him worthy of visitation and remembrance must be understood as other than the one to whom these things were given by him. How then is there still "one Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Ephesians 4:5)? For even if the difference between the natures is great, the manner of the union has shown that the Son who is from both is one. So if we say that he was thought worthy of remembrance by God the Word, we are surely natural men without the Spirit, as it is written (Jude 1:19); for we divide the one into two.

But if he was at the beginning what he is, Emmanuel from the womb itself, then, if we will not accept the manner of the union, the Word will surely be remembering himself; he will have thought himself worthy of the visitation and will be seen to have done himself a kindness. The force of these ideas will bring a great absurdity upon us, for his body is not foreign to the Word. Besides, who then is the one whom Holy Scripture says emptied himself? If, setting the one born of the holy Virgin apart, they say that he underwent the self-emptying, how was he emptied while being glorified, if indeed for a man like us it is honor and glory to be thought worthy of visitation and remembrance and to attain union with God? And if they were to say that the self-emptying of the Only-begotten was carried out in him, then he was emptied by undergoing something; for the matter of self-emptying would rather fit the one to whom suffering happened. So we have been saved by our own kind, if indeed the one born of the holy Virgin is a man like us, not united by hypostasis to the Word who sprang from God, as they themselves say. How then is Christ God, if he too, with us, has been thought worthy of remembrance from God and has become one of those who receive benefits? And yet we come to him as to God, praying and asking him to supply good things from above, as the one who grants requests to the whole creation in a manner befitting God.

"Since therefore the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise" (Hebrews 2:14). Before anything else, I think, we must look closely into what children the passage speaks of, which it says have shared in flesh and blood, and who it is that likewise took part in the same things.
